identity.title: LLM Fingerprinting via Semantically Conditioned Watermarks

problem.claim: Enable LLM owners to detect a fingerprint and verify ownership from responses to prompts in a semantic domain.

gap.claim: Existing query-key fingerprinting can fail after finetuning or quantization and may be detected and filtered from responses.

contributions.claim: Introduces semantically conditioned fingerprinting that replaces fixed query sets with a broad semantic domain and atypical keys with a statistical watermark diffused throughout responses.
Conditions watermarking on prompts from a predetermined domain, such as French, so domain-specific queries can be used for fingerprint detection and ownership verification.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that their approach introduces semantically conditioned watermarks for LLM fingerprinting.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the fingerprint is stealthy and robust to all common deployment scenarios in their experimental evaluation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Existing methods train responses to a few fixed queries with predefined atypical keys.
Such memorized keys may not survive finetuning or quantization and can be detected and filtered.
The method uses a broad semantic domain and a distributed statistical watermark instead of fixed queries and brittle keys.
The authors report stealth and robustness across common deployment scenarios, with domain-specific detection enabling ownership verification.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns the proposed mechanism with the stated failure modes: semantic conditioning broadens trigger coverage, while a distributed statistical signal replaces easily identifiable atypical keys.

lessons.interpretation: A mechanism-to-failure-mode mapping can make a technical proposal's motivation and intended benefits easy to assess.
lessons.application: When presenting a robustness-oriented method, explicitly pair each design change with the specific weakness it is meant to address.
lessons.exception: This framing is insufficient when the abstract does not provide evidence isolating which design change explains each reported outcome.

unknowns: No quantitative results, baselines, deployment conditions, or definitions of stealth and robustness are provided.
The abstract does not specify how the semantic domain is selected, how detection is performed, or how ownership verification is calibrated.
The claim of robustness covers “all common deployment scenarios,” but the scenarios are not enumerated.
